title: OPT 374 Human Visual Perception — Curated Foundations Question Bank

objectives.statement: Distinguish immediate sensory detection from the organization and interpretation that constitute perception.
Explain how bottom-up sensory evidence and top-down context, expectations and prior experience interact in visual perception.
Interpret reversible figures and visual illusions using figure-ground organization, context and depth cues.
Trace visual information from environmental light through the eye, retina and central visual pathways while relating anatomy, physiology and perceptual output.
Identify the major retinal layers, neuronal classes, optic disc and retinal nerve fibre layer and relate each to signal processing or clinical observation.
Explain the direction of light and neural signals through the inverted retina and the roles of photoreceptors, bipolar cells and ganglion cells.
Compare rods, cones and melanopsin-expressing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells by stimulus range, response role and visual function.
Relate foveal cone packing, displaced inner retinal layers, low convergence and vascular arrangement to high acuity and colour discrimination.
Compare midget, parasol and small bistratified retinal ganglion-cell pathways and predict their contributions to spatial, temporal and chromatic processing.
Explain how retinal convergence changes sensitivity, spatial resolution and the precision with which a signal can be localized.
Explain centre-surround antagonism and lateral inhibition and apply them to local contrast phenomena without treating simplified demonstrations as a complete account of perception.
Compare scotopic, mesopic and photopic vision and explain the sequence and mechanisms of light and dark adaptation.
Map crossed and uncrossed retinal inputs to the six principal LGN layers and preserve the separation of eye-of-origin signals.
Compare magnocellular, parvocellular and koniocellular streams by retinal origin, receptive-field scale and dominant visual information.
Identify V1, its principal laminar inputs and its relationship to the calcarine sulcus, optic radiations and retinotopic visual-field representation.
Analyze orientation, direction and end-stopping responses and distinguish simple, complex and end-stopped receptive-field properties.
Explain ocular dominance, ocular-dominance columns and the importance of early binocular experience for cortical development and amblyopia.
Interpret near, far and zero disparity tuning and explain how retinotopy preserves spatial relationships through V1.
Explain how extrastriate processing becomes progressively specialized and integrated beyond V1.
Compare the dorsal vision-for-action stream with the ventral vision-for-perception stream and relate each to parietal or temporal processing.
Localize characteristic motion, face and object-recognition deficits to relevant extrastriate networks while distinguishing selective perceptual loss from ocular disease.
Interpret cortical blindness, hemispatial neglect and blindsight using the distinction between conscious visual perception, attention and subcortical visual responses.
Distinguish the retinogeniculocortical image-forming route from non-image-forming retinal projections that support circadian and pupillary responses.

questions.author: Optometry Study Hub slide-aligned content team
questions.sampleAnswer: The dorsal stream projects from occipital visual areas toward parietal cortex and transforms visual information into spatial coordinates for actions such as reaching and grasping. A dorsal lesion can produce optic ataxia or related difficulty guiding the hand despite recognizing the object. The ventral stream projects toward inferior temporal cortex and supports detailed form and object identity. A ventral lesion can produce visual agnosia or prosopagnosia despite adequate basic vision. These dissociations support specialized perception and action systems, although normal behaviour depends on interaction between them.
rubric: Identifies the dorsal stream as projecting mainly toward parietal cortex and supporting spatial guidance/visually guided action.
Identifies the ventral stream as projecting mainly toward temporal cortex and supporting object/form/identity perception.
Provides a defensible dorsal-stream example such as optic ataxia or severe spatial-action impairment.
Provides a defensible ventral-stream example such as visual agnosia or prosopagnosia.
States that the streams are specialized but interacting rather than completely independent.
